Scrotal Pain and Masses

painful scrotum and painless mass: separate workups · torsion vs epididymitis · the two hard pairs · tumor markersWas the onset sudden or gradual, and does the mass transilluminate or change with Valsalva?

1Presentation2Urgent3Differential4Workup5Criteria6Severity7Treatment8Follow-upPractice
1Presentation
Bottom line
  • Sudden pain, a high-riding transverse testis and no cremasteric reflex is torsion: straight to surgery; imaging only when the exam is equivocal
  • Pain building over days with fever, dysuria and tenderness behind the testis is epididymitis, diagnosed clinically: treat without imaging
  • A painless mass is sorted by transillumination, position and Valsalva; a firm mass on the testis is a tumor: ultrasound and markers, then inguinal orchiectomy
What it is

Scrotal pain or a scrotal mass in a boy or young man

Sort by

Painful: onset, location, cremasteric reflex painless: transillumination, position, Valsalva

Hands off

A right or fixed varicocele in a young child: Abdominal Mass in a Young Child; purpura with scrotal pain: Bruising and Purpura in a Child

2Urgent risks
TorsionSudden severe pain, nausea and vomiting, a high-riding transverse testis, no cremasteric reflex

If the exam fits, choose emergent detorsion with bilateral orchiopexy; no waiting for imaging; salvage window about 6 hours.

Undescended testisAn acute abdomen in a boy with an empty scrotum: intra-abdominal torsion
Fournier gangreneToxic, crepitus, necrosis; diabetic

If there is crepitus or necrosis, choose emergent debridement.

3Differential
The acute scrotum, most tempting first
DiagnosisFingerprintDecides it
Testicular torsionAge 12 to 18, bell-clapper deformity; nausea and vomiting, no fever; pain worse on lifting the testisMinutes to hours; high-riding transverse testis; cremasteric reflex absent
EpididymitisPosterior tenderness, dysuria, fever, pyuria; pain eases on lifting the testis (Prehn sign) Epididymitis by ageOver 35 or at low risk of a sexually transmitted infection, the organism is usually Escherichia coli: levofloxacin or trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole.Days; reflex intact; under 35, chlamydia or gonorrhea
Torsion of the appendix testisPrepubertal boy; blue dot at the upper poleGradual; reflex intact; supportive care
OrchitisMumps in an unvaccinated boy; sterility risk in teenagersDays, after parotitis; reflex intact; supportive
IgA vasculitis (Henoch-Schönlein purpura)
Palpable purpura on the buttocks and legs, joint and belly pain, after a coldDays; the rash, with scrotal pain
The painless scrotal mass, most tempting first
DiagnosisFingerprintDecides it
HydrocelePainless, uniform; in an infant, larger by midday if communicatingTransilluminates; the testis is felt within
Varicocele VaricoceleThe left gonadal vein meets the left renal vein at a right angle, and the aorta and the superior mesenteric artery can pinch the renal vein; the right one joins the inferior vena cava at a slant. A raised scrotal temperature impairs spermatogenesis, and a varicocele may also shrink the testis on its side. A new left varicocele can follow a left renal vein thrombosis. Older men not seeking fertility: scrotal support and nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs.Bag of worms, about 90% left-sidedLarger standing or with Valsalva, smaller supine; does not transilluminate
Indirect inguinal herniaEnlarges with Valsalva; soft tissue or bowelReducible, and you cannot get above it
SpermatoceleAbove and separate from the testis, like a varicoceleTransilluminates; no change with position or Valsalva
Testicular tumor Tumor markersA raised alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) means a yolk sac, embryonal or teratoma component, never a pure seminoma. Beta human chorionic gonadotropin (beta-hCG) can rise in either kind; only AFP excludes. Both normal with a solid mass: a pure seminoma or a stromal tumor (Leydig, Sertoli), separated by a hormonal syndrome. Lactate dehydrogenase tracks tumor burden, not histology. A teratoma, heterogeneous with calcified and cystic areas on ultrasound, is malignant in adults whatever its maturity and benign in prepubertal boys; it resists chemotherapy, so residual masses are resected. A Leydig cell tumor, a mostly benign stromal tumor with Reinke crystals, shows itself by its hormones; a Sertoli cell tumor, also stromal and usually benign, is typically hormonally silent.Firm, fixed, painless, on the testis; seminoma is the commonest; cryptorchidism or Klinefelter syndrome raises the riskDoes not transilluminate; solid on ultrasound
4Workup
Clues that change the answer
CluePoints toNext move
Empty scrotum since birth, more often after preterm birth; the testis cannot be brought downCryptorchidism: torsion and seminoma risk, even after repairOrchiopexy at 6 months to 2 years
Transilluminating mass in an infantCongenital hydrocele through a patent processus vaginalis; most close in 12 monthsObserve; repair if it persists or a hernia comes with it
Under 35 or sexually active, with epididymitisChlamydia or gonorrheaCeftriaxone plus doxycycline
Adolescent varicocele, testis over 20% smallerSurgical indicationLigation or embolization
Testicular mass with gynecomastia or early puberty; markers normalLeydig cell tumor
Ultrasound, then inguinal orchiectomy
Groin bulge below the inguinal ligament in an older womanFemoral hernia; it cannot reach the scrotumPrompt repair: high incarceration risk

Pause point. The bait: Doppler ultrasound before surgery for a classic torsion, or imaging for a classic epididymitis. The exam decides both; imaging is for the equivocal torsion.

Practice
  1. Right-sided varicocele, sudden onset, or one that fails to decompress supine → Retroperitoneal mass or RCC invading the renal vein → abdominal computed tomography
  2. Mass transilluminates with the testis palpable within → Hydrocele → observe (infantile hydroceles usually close by age 1)
  3. Reducible mass extending from the inguinal canal, can't get above it → Indirect inguinal hernia → repair
  4. Firm, fixed, on the testis, no positional change → Ultrasound + AFP, β-hCG, LDH → radical inguinal orchiectomy (never transscrotal – it seeds lymphatics). Cryptorchidism is the biggest risk factor, for both testes
  5. Small transilluminating cyst at the superior pole, unchanging → Spermatocele → reassurance
  6. Adolescent with a varicocele and >20% testicular volume discrepancy → Refer for ligation
  7. Groin bulge below the inguinal ligament in an older woman → Femoral hernia → prompt repair
  8. Sudden severe pain, high-riding transverse testis, absent cremasteric reflex → Testicular torsion → emergent surgery
  9. 4 yo M, painless soft scrotal mass superior to the right testicle that does not decompress supine, blood pressure 160/96 → Secondary varicocele from an abdominal mass → abdominal ultrasonography
Transferable rules A 3-day timeline of scrotal pain excludes torsion. When the clinical findings confirm infection well enough, treat rather than image. Also, read the grammatical form of the answer choices before the stem. If every choice is an anatomic process, the question asks for mechanism; if every choice is a test, the next diagnostic step; if every choice is a drug, treatment.
